standouts.title: Become a $1M/yr FDE (Full Course)
standouts.summary: Greg Isenberg interviews Vas from Varick on what it actually takes to put AI to work inside a real company. Vas's thesis: AI pays off through process reengineering first, agents second. His forward-deployed engineers run interviews, process mining, and step sorting, then build agents inside the client's existing systems of record. Case studies include a $5B public software company, a PE portfolio rollout, and a 60-person accounting firm; one AP overhaul cut cost per invoice from $31 to $6. The back half covers the three skills of a top FDE, why they earn so much, a five-day starter plan, sidekick vs background agents, and the emerging on-premise hardware demand from regulated clients.
args: Reengineer the process, then deploy agents. Most failed AI pilots automate a broken workflow. Vas's method maps every step, sorts them into four buckets, and only then decides what becomes code, what becomes an agent, and what stays human.

Build inside systems of record, not alongside them. Agents that live in NetSuite, the AP system, or the CRM inherit trust, permissions, and workflow; agents bolted on the side inherit nothing. This is the data-readiness argument made operational.

The FDE is the business model, not the job title. The economics work because FDEs sell outcomes priced against cost-per-invoice-type metrics, and the AI roll-up angle (buy a boring business, reengineer it) turns the same method into an equity play.
standouts.why: This is the clearest public description of the Alpha Infra operating model I've seen, and it landed two days after you started the consulting push. Three direct uses: (a) productize your diagnostic into Vas's sequence (interviews, process map, step sort, agents in systems of record) and name it something; (b) the $31-to-$6 AP stat and the 60-person accounting-firm case study are LinkedIn gold from your CA tribe's home turf; (c) the five-day starter plan is a template for your entry offer. The question it surfaces: does your current pilot process look disciplined like this, or are you still selling the capability before mapping the process? Also note the pair with yesterday's governance thread: "when to use code, agents, or humans" is the same decision tree your agent-governance assessment would sell.

standouts.title: Trump's Super Intelligence Summit, AI Safety Accord, GDP Beats, Midterm Predictions
standouts.summary: The Besties open with a behind-the-scenes account of Trump's Super Intelligence Summit: how the accord was created, negotiated, and signed. From there: the cybersecurity arms race, data centers as national-security infrastructure, America.gov, and coordinated "doomer" messaging. The data segment covers the upward GDP revision, jobs, inflation coming in soft, rates, manufacturing, and diesel. Closes with midterm predictions and a 2028 look-ahead.
args: The accord is signed and voluntary. A federal-level AI safety accord now exists on paper, which is exactly the shape of policy that starts as opt-in and becomes a client procurement checkbox within a year. The Besties' behind-the-scenes account suggests it was driven more by optics than teeth, which is itself the signal: the floor will rise later, without a vote.

Data centers have been re-framed as national-security infrastructure. That framing puts the whole bubble-vs-nation-building debate on new footing: the capex skeptics (see the Eisman episode below) are now arguing against something DC has blessed as strategic.

The economy keeps beating the gloom. Upward GDP revision, soft inflation print, 162K August payrolls: the "your clients have budget" reading is still intact, and AI spend is coming from operating cash flow, not hope.
standouts.why: This continues the week's policy thread from Thursday's FTC-probe episode and gives it a third act: probe, meeting, signed accord. For your consulting: the governance question for clients just moved from "should we have an AI policy" to "which version of the accord's principles shows up in your procurement requirements first." Content angle: a LinkedIn post contrasting the voluntary accord with the FTC's enforcement posture, framed as the two forces that will define AI procurement in 2027. And the midterms segment is worth 15 minutes for anyone watching how the 2026 results re-route AI policy staffing.

standouts.title: Steve Eisman: One Company Could Break The AI Boom
standouts.summary: Ed Elson hosts Steve Eisman (of Big Short fame), who argues Anthropic and OpenAI are manufacturing a crisis narrative. He wouldn't invest in the Anthropic IPO, explains what he'll scrutinize when the S-1 finally drops, lays out why high yields could force a market correction, and reveals one company he's shorting plus his current positioning.
args: The "crisis" is a lobbying tactic, not a balance-sheet event. Eisman's read: the labs' urgency about compute, safety, and scale is partly aimed at policymakers and capital providers, manufacturing the conditions for the funding they need. The Anthropic IPO, on this view, is the exit the narrative is building toward.

The S-1 is the moment of truth. What matters isn't the growth story, it's unit economics: revenue per seat, retention, and whether the spend-everything training strategy compounds or just burns. This rhymes with the leaked Anthropic financials from Thursday's episode.

High yields are the correction trigger, not AI itself. Eisman's macro call is that rates, not a tech repricing, are what finally bite — and he's positioned (including one active short) for the market to get that wrong first.
standouts.why: No investment action implied here, just the questions worth carrying into client conversations: if the capex buildout is circular (labs fund infra that serves the labs), your clients' AI budgets inherit that fragility. The useful pairing is with All-In this week: Eisman says the crisis is manufactured; the Summit says the buildout is national strategy. Both can be true, and the gap between them is where your clients' actual risk sits. Watch for the real Anthropic S-1 against Eisman's checklist — it's the single best document coming for how AI businesses really make money.

standouts.title: Willpower Expert: The Secret To Effortless Discipline - Angela Duckworth - #1158
standouts.summary: Chris Williamson interviews psychologist Angela Duckworth on what she's learned since writing Grit: whether removing friction from our lives is making us weaker, how much physical environments matter (and when to change them), how to tell an environment problem from a willpower problem, and how to engineer your surroundings to enhance grit.
args: Stop diagnosing willpower; diagnose the environment. Duckworth's updated thesis: when a habit fails, the first suspect is the room, not your resolve. The disciplined people she studies mostly don't wrestle temptation — they never meet it.
Friction removal has a cost. Making everything effortless trains the muscle for nothing; the question isn't whether to add friction, it's where to place it deliberately.

Changing environments beats changing minds. Moving, rearranging, or re-architecting the defaults you live inside does more for grit than any motivational intervention — and it's cheaper than the coaching-industrial complex.
standouts.why: Q4 starts this week, and this is the environment-design episode to act on once: instead of negotiating with yourself about training, phone time, and work blocks, redesign the room they're fought in. It also pairs with last week's Sulek episode, but Duckworth adds the diagnostic you were missing — ask "is this a willpower problem or an environment problem" before adding another system. Parenting angle for the twins' second birthday today: grit is cultivable, and modeled persistence plus a well-designed environment beats lectures. At 101 minutes it's long; the environment chapters are the ones to keep.
